chunks: "Ripple matters on both sides of the converter. On the load side, ripple eats into the supply tolerance. If a 1.
0 volts core allows plus or minus 3%, that's 30 millivolts each way, and 17 millivolts peak-to-peak of ripple uses 8.
5 millivolts of that, over a quarter, before DC error and transients.
Worse, sensitive circuits convert ripple into errors: an ADC's reference or supply ripple appears as noise or spurs, and a VCO or PLL has supply pushing.
Say 5 megahertz per volt of pushing: 10 millivolts of ripple at 500 kilohertz offset gives a modulation index of 0.
1 and a spur about 26 decibels below the carrier before any filtering, which is awful for RF. Even with 40 decibels of rejection it's minus 66 dBc, still marginal.

On the converter side, ripple current means higher peak current, so a bigger saturation margin and current-limit headroom, more core loss in the inductor, ripple heating in the capacitors, and more conducted EMI at the switching frequency and harmonics.
So I reduce ripple to the level the load needs: more inductance, capacitance, frequency, interleaving or a post filter.
But each costs size, efficiency or money, so a digital core with a wide tolerance may not need much."
